title: Uddalaka and Shvetaketu: "you've studied twelve years — do you know That?" (6.1)
hook: a son comes home after twelve years of study, proud and stiff, and his father asks him one question he can't answer
tomorrow: the clay, the gold, the iron

segments.voice: Yesterday: pancagni, the king's picture of the whole cycle of life. Your line was rain to food to seed to person. Did you taste the rain in a meal? Day three hundred thirty-nine.
screen: `PANCAGNI — RAIN TO FOOD TO SEED TO PERSON.`

segments.voice: The front door opens. A young man comes home after twelve years away. He's twenty-four. He has memorized the Vedas. He walks in, the text says, swollen with pride, thinking himself very learned, a little stiff with it. Maybe you've met him. Maybe you've been him, home from the first year of college, correcting everyone at dinner. His father watches him for a while. And then he asks a question. Not a test of memory. One question. Today begins the sixth chapter of the Chandogya Upanishad, one of the most studied in Hindu philosophy: a father, a son, and a series of lessons that will run for the next two weeks.
screen: `HOME AFTER TWELVE YEARS.` → `SWOLLEN WITH PRIDE.` → `ONE QUESTION.`

segments.voice: The father is Uddalaka Aruni, one of the great teachers of the Upanishads. The son is Shvetaketu, the same young man the king embarrassed yesterday. The chapter begins twelve years earlier, when Shvetaketu is twelve, and his father sends him off to study with a warning: in our family, nobody is a brahmin just by birth. Go and learn. Now he's back, proud of all he knows. And his father asks him: since you think so much of yourself, did you ask for that teaching by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, and the unknown becomes known? Shvetaketu has no idea what he means. How could there be such a teaching, sir? Sit with the question for a moment. It isn't asking for one more fact. Twelve years of facts are already in Shvetaketu's head. It's asking whether there's one thing that, once you know it, makes everything else make sense. A key, not another room. The Upanishads have a name for what that key opens. They often just call it That. And the father is gentle about it. He doesn't mock. He uses a word he'll repeat through all the lessons ahead: somya, my dear, the way you'd talk to someone you love. Then he begins to teach, with things from the kitchen and the garden: clay, salt, honey, a seed. Over the next two weeks the lessons keep coming, and nine times the father closes one with the same three words. Tomorrow, the first: a lump of clay.
screen: `TWELVE YEARS EARLIER, A WARNING.` · `THE UNHEARD BECOMES HEARD.` · `A KEY, NOT ANOTHER ROOM.` · `SOMYA, MY DEAR.` · then, large: `THE ONE THING WORTH KNOWING.`

segments.voice: Today's practice sets down what you know. Sit and settle. Let the facts come up: your job, your skills, your opinions, what you studied. Notice how much is there. Then, one by one, set them down beside you, like books on a table. You can pick them all up later. For now, sit with empty hands, and let the father's question hang in the air, without answering it. The bell holds the time.
Somya, gentle, dear. Uddalaka's word for his son, repeated through the lessons, as he asks whether anyone taught him the one teaching by which the unknown becomes known.
Your line: the one thing worth knowing. Today, ask someone wiser than you what they think is the one thing worth knowing, and just listen. Day three hundred thirty-nine.

screen: `DAY 339 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE CLAY, THE GOLD, THE IRON.`

howItsDone: The sixth chapter of the Chandogya is one of the most studied texts in Hindu philosophy; Vedanta teachers often walk students through Uddalaka's lessons one at a time.

the teaching he never asked for

fork.setup: you're Uddalaka. your son is home after twelve years, proud of everything he's memorized. what do you do?
options: praise him and throw a feast.
ask him whether he learned the teaching by which the unknown becomes known.
quiz him on the Vedas until he gets one wrong.
fork.reveal: one question, asked gently. Shvetaketu has no answer, and the most famous lessons of the Chandogya begin.

original.note: Sanskrit somya: gentle, dear. Uddalaka's word for his son, repeated through the lessons.

trapdoor: what you thought: a father taking his know-it-all son down a peg.
what it means: a question about the one thing that makes everything else known, asked with love.
what a scholar hears: Chandogya 6.1.3, the opening of Uddalaka's teaching; the chapter's refrain is tat tvam asi, said nine times by one common count.
recall: God's gift of love and help, freely given

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 6.1.1–3 (Shvetaketu sent at twelve, returns at twenty-four; the question)

notes: Ages (twelve when sent, twenty-four on return) per 6.1.2; confirm.
Identification of this Shvetaketu with the one questioned by Pravahana Jaivali (5.3): both are Shvetaketu Aruneya, son of Gautama/Uddalaka; confirm.
Refrain count: tat tvam asi occurs nine times in 6.8–6.16 by a common count; the script says 'most of them end with the same three words' and 'nine lessons'. Confirm.
'That' (tat) as the Upanishads' name for the ultimate is a simplification; confirm phrasing.

Audit (10% sample): hook no longer opens on 'graduation day' (day 389's graduation-speech image); 'the most famous chapter' softened to 'one of the most studied'; 'nine lessons, most of them end' corrected to 'nine times the father closes one' with the refrain, since the clay lesson that starts tomorrow is not one of the nine refrain lessons.
